Multiple studies identify peak current as the dominant factor for MRR (86.43% effect in one ANOVA) and show pulse-on time as the next-most important parameter in Taguchi designs. (Nas & Kara 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2022) 
Separate ANOVA work on EDM also reports amperage as overwhelmingly influential for MRR (99.66% in that study). (Akıncıoğlu 2022) 
In short, studies consistently agree that increasing peak current (amperage) and longer pulse-on time raise MRR; the exact relative importance varies by study and experimental design. (Nas & Kara 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2022)

### Peak current (amperage)
Multiple experimental studies found that peak current (amperage) dominates MRR, explaining the largest share of variance in designed experiments. (Nas & Kara 2022)(Akıncıoğlu 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2022) 

### Pulse-on time / pulse duration
Pulse-on time or pulse duration is repeatedly identified as a major driver of MRR alongside current, and is frequently the second-most important factor in Taguchi and factorial studies. (Nas & Kara 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2022) 

### Electrode material / grain size (secondary influence)
Electrode material and its properties (for example graphite grain size) affect process efficiency and thus MRR, with finer-grained graphite reported to increase process efficiency and reduce tool wear under comparable electrical conditions. (Nowicki et al. 2024)(Nowicki et al. 2022)

(Tan et al. 2018) Aging produces massive needle-shaped nanoprecipitates Ni$_3$X (X = Ti, Al, Mo) in the martensitic matrix that provide age hardening via Orowan bowing and coherency-strain mechanisms. (Tan et al. 2018) Heat treatments (solution/aging) significantly relieve residual stress and reduce build-orientation mechanical anisotropy. (Tan et al. 2018) Aging yields maximum nano-hardness and precipitation is the main control on both hardness and corrosion potential. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) Intercritical tempering near austenite-forming temperatures can induce reversed austenite, which precipitates mainly along martensite-lath boundaries driven by local Ni enrichment and improves pitting resistance. (Khan et al. 2022) Prior heat treatment also changes the morphology and integrity of subsequent nitride layers during plasma nitriding. (Godec et al. 2021)
rows.b:
Heat treatment transforms as-built SLM maraging steel from a highly refined, as-printed martensitic microstructure with high residual stress into a precipitate-strengthened and (depending on temperature) partially reverted-austenite-containing microstructure, while relieving residual stresses and altering hardness and corrosion behaviour. (Tan et al. 2018)

Microstructure of the as-printed state
- As-printed SLM maraging steel is a fine-grained martensitic matrix with submicron grain size and high cooling rates, containing little or no equilibrium precipitates. (Tan et al. 2018)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Precipitation and age hardening after conventional ageing
- Ageing produces massive needle-shaped nanoprecipitates (Ni3X, X = Ti, Al, Mo) inside the martensitic matrix that provide age hardening via Orowan bowing and coherency strain mechanisms, and ageing gives maximum nano-hardness. (Tan et al. 2018)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

Stress relief and anisotropy change
- Heat treatments significantly relieve residual stresses induced by SLM and slightly reduce the build-orientation mechanical anisotropy observed in as-fabricated parts. (Tan et al. 2018)

Solution treatment, nitriding and combined effects
- Prior solution treatment and ageing change the response to subsequent thermochemical treatments: nitriding without prior ageing produced cracks in the nitride compound layer, whereas nitriding after prior heat treatment improved wear and corrosion resistance. (Godec et al. 2021)

Intercritical treatment and austenite reversion
- Intercritical heat treatment around the α′+γ range (example: 720°C) produces reversed austenite that precipitates mainly along martensite lath boundaries, driven by local Ni enrichment from dissolved intermetallics, and this reversed austenite increases pitting resistance in chloride solution tests. (Khan et al. 2022)

AM-specific in situ effects
- The SLM process itself can act as an intrinsic heat treatment causing in situ tempering and precipitation and producing hierarchical subgrain structures and fine precipitates that differentiate AM microstructures from conventional counterparts. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)

### What these sources do not cover
- Quantitative kinetics (time–temperature–precipitate size curves) and detailed phase-fraction evolution during specific heat-treatment schedules. (Tan et al. 2018)

SLM maraging steel’s corrosion behaviour is influenced strongly by its as-built microstructure and subsequent heat/thermo-chemical treatments: heat treatments, precipitation state and reversed austenite can improve corrosion/pitting resistance, while improper treatments (e.g. nitriding without prior aging) can cause defects that worsen performance. (Khan et al. 2022)(Godec et al. 2021)

Evidence and synthesis:
- Reversed austenite formed by intercritical tempering (720 °C) raised pitting potential and lowered corrosion current density and corrosion rate in 3.5 wt% NaCl, i.e. improved pitting resistance. (Khan et al. 2022)
- Precipitation (age hardening) and the precipitation state govern both hardness and corrosion behaviour, with aging producing the maximum nano-hardness and lowest corrosion potential in one study. (Tan et al. 2018)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)
- Plasma nitriding improved wear and corrosion resistance when applied after prior heat treatments, but nitriding without prior aging produced cracks in the compound layer that are detrimental. (Godec et al. 2021)
- A review concludes that AM’s unique microstructures (hierarchical (sub)grains and fine precipitates) can enhance corrosion resistance relative to conventional steels, though results across studies are not uniform. (Haghdadi et al. 2020)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

What remains only partially answered: comparative quantitative corrosion rates across environments and long-term chloride performance beyond the cited NaCl pitting tests are not fully reported in these passages. (Khan et al. 2022)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

SLM maraging steel shows fine as-built martensitic microstructures and its corrosion behaviour is strongly influenced by heat treatments, reversed austenite formation, surface finish, and thermochemical treatments. (Tan et al. 2018)

### Microstructure and baseline corrosion
As-built SLM maraging steel is nearly fully dense with a fine martensitic structure and nanoprecipitates, observations that underpin comparisons of corrosion behaviour. (Yap et al. 2015)(Tan et al. 2018) 

### Effect of heat treatment and aging
Heat treatments (solution + aging) change precipitate state, relieve residual stress, and alter corrosion behaviour, with aging producing maximum nano-hardness and lowest corrosion potential in the studies reporting such metrics. (Tan et al. 2018)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) 

### Reversed austenite improves pitting resistance
Intercritical tempering that produces reversed austenite (e.g. tempering near 720°C) increased pitting potential and reduced corrosion current density and corrosion rate in 3.5 wt% NaCl, indicating enhanced pitting resistance when reversed austenite is present. (Khan et al. 2022) 

### Surface finish and electropolishing
Despite a finer microstructure, heat-treated SLM and conventional wrought maraging steels showed similar nano-hardness and corrosion behaviour in the reported comparisons, and electropolishing reduced SLM surface roughness (Ra) by 65%, an action likely to affect corrosion performance via smoother surfaces. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) 

### Thermochemical treatment: nitriding
Plasma nitriding can improve wear and corrosion resistance of SLM 18Ni-300 when applied after prior aging or solution/aging heat treatments, whereas nitriding without prior aging produced cracks in the compound nitride layer. (Godec et al. 2021) 

### Agreement and differences across studies
Studies consistently attribute corrosion changes to microstructure, precipitates, and surface state, and they agree that appropriate post-processing (aging, reversed-austenite tempering, electropolishing, or nitriding after heat treatment) can improve corrosion or pitting resistance. (Tan et al. 2018)(Khan et al. 2022)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)(Godec et al. 2021) Differences lie in which post-process (reversion versus nitriding versus electropolish) is emphasized and in the corrosion metrics reported. (Khan et al. 2022)(Godec et al. 2021)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) 

### What these sources do not cover
Long-term chloride immersion corrosion kinetics and standardized comparative corrosion rates are not provided in these sources. (Khan et al. 2022)
